extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in aesthetics and the social/moral value of art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying aesthetic, moral, and social criteria for judging artworks and the institution/practice of art (definitions of beauty, aims of art, ethical costs, and who art serves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience relevance / For whom is it done
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctively the question presents itself—For whom is this being done? Whom _can_ it please?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should be assessed by whether it genuinely pleases or benefits a real audience; if the work only gratifies a narrow, affected, or socially derivative group (e.g., 'some young footman or depraved artisan' who imitates upper-class tastes), the work's value is doubtful. Examples/anti-patterns: elaborate stage trappings that leave real people 'at a loss' suggest art disconnected from any genuine audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity versus Superfluous Theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are, occasionally, good melodies in the opera, to which it is pleasant to listen, they could have been sung simply, without these stupid costumes and all the processions and recitatives and hand-wavings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether ornamentation (costumes, processions, ritualised gesture) is necessary to the artistic effect or merely gratuitous. Anti-pattern: elaborate spectacle that obscures or substitutes for intrinsic musical or poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral character of content
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballet, in which half-naked women make voluptuous movements... is simply a lewd performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a work's content is morally harmful or corrupting. Works that provoke sensuality or degrade moral sensibilities may be judged negatively on moral grounds, not merely aesthetic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of social/labour sacrifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, for the sake of which the labour of millions, the lives of men, and above all, love between man and man, are being sacrificed,—this very art is becoming something more and more vague and uncertain to human perception... it is necessary for a society ... to find out whether all that professes to be art is really art; whether (as is presupposed in our society) all that which is art is good; and whether it is important and worth those sacrifices which it necessitates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When art demands significant social or economic cost (subsidies, labour exploitation), it must be held to stricter standards: authenticity (is it genuine art?), moral worth (is it good?), and social importance (is it worth the sacrifice?). Anti-pattern: accepting any production labelled 'art' as deserving public support without scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: is it really art?
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary ... to find out whether all that professes to be art is really art;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere crafts, entertainments, or social display from genuine art. Question practices and productions that claim the title without substance. Use criteria (see other entries: beauty, goodness, social function) to test authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral value: is art good?
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether (as is presupposed in our society) all that which is art is good;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess art for its moral implications and whether it promotes or undermines goodness. This is an explicit standard adopted by some aesthetic theories (see Sulzer, Mendelssohn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social importance / Worthiness of investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it is important and worth those sacrifices which it necessitates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the cultural/social benefits of an artwork or institution justify public or private expenditure and the labour required to produce it. Example: massive state subsidies should be justified by demonstrable communal value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as production of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is such activity as produces beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classical criterion treats art's purpose as making beauty manifest. Use judgments about form, harmony, expression, and sensory pleasure to evaluate works under this conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of the five senses / broad scope of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Kralik and Guyau: the arts of taste, smell, touch, hearing, and sight are aesthetic; e.g. the art of cookery, costume, perfume, and touch (velvet softness) can be aesthetic achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict 'art' to visual or literary forms; evaluate sensory crafts (cooking, costume, perfumery, tactile design) by their capacity to create aesthetic unity and convey an Idea. Anti-pattern: dismissing sensory arts as 'not art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and coherence of the concept of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: This strange conception 'beauty'... after whole mountains of books ... the question, What is beauty? remains to this day quite unsolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that 'beauty' is contested; a rigorous evaluation should make explicit which theory of beauty is being applied. Anti-pattern: invoking 'beauty' as a self-evident justification without definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baumgarten: Beauty as sensory-recognised Perfection; art imitates nature
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Baumgarten... the object of æsthetic (i.e. sensuous) knowledge is Beauty. Beauty is the Perfect (the Absolute), recognised through the senses... Baumgarten considers the highest embodiment of beauty is seen by us in nature, and he therefore thinks that the highest aim of art is to copy nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this standard evaluate fidelity to nature and harmonious arrangement of parts: does the work manifest 'sensuous perfection' and accurate/idealised imitation of natural forms? Anti-pattern: art that deliberately departs without justification from natural harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sulzer/Mendelssohn: Art's aim is Goodness / moral education
rubrics_metrics.description: They ... recognise as the aim of art, not beauty, but goodness... The aim of art is moral perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works by their capacity to evoke and educate moral feeling; aesthetic merit is subordinate to ethical contribution. Example: compare works that glorify virtue vs those that merely please the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winckelmann: Primacy of beauty (form, idea, expression) and classical imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law and aim of all art is beauty only ... three kinds of beauty: (1) beauty of form, (2) beauty of idea ... (3) beauty of expression ... highest aim of art ... attained in antique art; modern art should therefore aim at imitating ancient art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate form (formal proportions), idea (compositional conception), and expression (integration of form and idea). Consider classical models as standards of excellence under this view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and proportion (Shaftesbury)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is beautiful is harmonious and proportionable, what is harmonious and proportionable is true...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural relations, balance, and proportionality within the work. Anti-pattern: works exhibiting disjointed or disproportionate elements without compensatory intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity amid variety / Internal sense (Hutcheson)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of beauty consists in evoking in us the perception of uniformity amid variety. In the recognition of what is art we are guided by 'an internal sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work achieves coherence (unity) while offering variety and richness; consider intuitive 'internal sense' reactions as relevant data for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of effect / richness in narrow limits (Home / Lord Kames)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is that which is pleasant. The standard of true taste is that the maximum of richness, fulness, strength, and variety of impression should be contained in the narrowest limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that achieve intense, multifaceted impact with restraint and concision rather than bloated or diffuse treatments. Anti-pattern: maximum effect obtained through excess rather than craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of sublime/beautiful in human instincts (Burke)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime and beautiful ... have their origin in the promptings of self-preservation and of society... The first (self-preservation) is attained by nourishment, defence, and war; the second (society) by intercourse and propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sublime or beautiful effects, consider their relation to fundamental human drives—fear/self-preservation or sociability/sex-instinct—and how art evokes these deep responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as unification of dispersed natural beauties; role of taste and genius (Pagano)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art consists in uniting the beauties dispersed in nature. The capacity to perceive these beauties is taste, the capacity to bring them into one whole is artistic genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the artist's ability to select and synthesize elements from nature into coherent wholes; distinguish between mere perception (taste) and organizing creative power (genius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of perceptual ideas (Hemsterhuis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is that which gives most pleasure, and that gives most pleasure which gives us the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cognitive density and immediacy: does the work deliver rich associative/idea-provoking content efficiently? Anti-pattern: works that are prolix but ideationally thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian disinterestedness / Aesthetic pleasure without utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty, according to Kant, in its subjective meaning is that which, in general and necessarily, without reasonings and without practical advantage, pleases. In its objective meaning it is the form of a suitable object in so far as that object is perceived without any conception of its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess aesthetic value as pleasure independent of concept or practical benefit—a 'free' aesthetic judgment. Avoid conflating usefulness with beauty when applying this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity / Beautiful soul and educative aim (Fichte)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deformity or beauty of an object, according to Fichte, depends on the point of view of the observer. Beauty therefore exists, not in the world, but in the beautiful soul. Art is the manifestation of this beautiful soul, and its aim is the education ... of the whole man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the role of the observer's moral/spiritual condition in judgment; consider art's educative capacity to shape character and 'whole' human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical treatment of artists and labour conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: I heard the words, 'asses,' 'fools,' 'idiots,' 'swine,' addressed to the musicians and singers ... the unhappy individual ... physically and mentally demoralised ... does not reply, and does what is demanded of him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional and production practices: cruelty, humiliation, and exploitation of performers are grounds for negative judgment of artistic practice, regardless of claimed 'tradition' or outcomes. Anti-pattern: defending abusive conduct on the basis of 'musical tradition' or artistic 'greatness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of funding and exploitation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: They all need the help of workmen ... either through payments from rich people, or through subsidies given by Government ... This money is collected from the people, some of whom have to sell their only cow to pay the tax, and who never get those aesthetic pleasures which art gives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the economic and social means of producing art are just: public subsidies or private patronage that impoverish or exploit ordinary people must be justified by accessible benefit or redistributive fairness. Anti-pattern: concentrating luxurious artistic consumption among elites while the populace bears the cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and non-contradiction in critical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism... has latterly become so self-contradictory, that, if we exclude from the domain of art all that to which the critics of various schools themselves deny the title, there is scarcely any art left. The artists of various sects ... mutually exclude and destroy themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer critical frameworks that are coherent and stable enough to support public decisions (subsidies, reputational reward). Anti-pattern: relativistic critical pluralism that makes the category 'art' meaningless and undermines any claim to special social status.
